# Akbr Kanyesigye

> Akbr Kanyesigye, software and data engineer in Kampala. Census systems, data pipelines, dashboards, and AI that answers from Uganda's official statistics.

This is the full plain-text version of https://kanyeceejaya.github.io/, generated from the site on 2026-09-23. A shorter index lives at https://kanyeceejaya.github.io/llms.txt.

## About

I build the systems that move public data from collection to use.

Software and data engineer in Kampala. I work along the whole path a figure takes: the tools that collect it, the pipelines that process it, the dashboards that show it, and the AI that answers from it.

## Now

- **A prediction market for Africa**, in the spirit of Polymarket: markets on the questions people here actually argue about, settled on sources they can check.
- **Sanyu**, the Bureau's AI assistant over official statistics: more datasets, drafted statistical briefs, and a short code of practice for AI over official figures.
- **A harmonised data portal** that brings datasets from across government agencies into one place, so service delivery can rest on shared figures.
- **TuuraHub**, a property management product for East African landlords, in beta on the side.
- **Azure Data Fundamentals**, the next certificate after AWS Cloud Practitioner.

## Work

Grouped by who the work serves.

### Official statistics, at the Uganda Bureau of Statistics

#### [Sanyu](https://statistics.ubos.org/sanyu) (2024 to now, AI)

Uganda's AI assistant for official statistics.

Ask a question in plain language, in English or one of five Ugandan languages, and get the figure with its source, a live table or chart, or a drafted statistical brief. The language model decides what to retrieve; the statistical database decides what the value is. No figure reaches the reader unless a structured query returned it, and every figure carries its table, survey, period and geography.

- 5,100+: indicators from six official sources
- 1,600+: tables lifted from published reports, citeable by page
- 40 ms: cold start, down from 30 to 60 seconds
- 45: golden-fact regression tests on every build

Built with Node.js, SQLite, LLM tool calling, RAG, MCP endpoints, Python pipelines, Nginx and pm2. Built in-house at UBOS with Sunbird AI on the language side.

Links: [statistics.ubos.org/sanyu](https://statistics.ubos.org/sanyu)

Screenshot: Sanyu's chat screen: a sidebar of data sources such as Census 2024 and CPI, and the prompt 'Ask Sanyu about Uganda's official statistics' (https://kanyeceejaya.github.io/images/shot-sanyu.jpg)

#### Census e-recruitment and field staff management (2023 to 2024, web platform)

The system behind the people who counted Uganda in 2024.

Applications, vetting, shortlists, interviews, assignment and payroll records for the National Population and Housing Census, decentralised to every district, with national dashboards for the Bureau. I was the primary developer and ran its deployment.

- 200,000+: census personnel managed nationwide
- 80%: faster issue resolution from the testing and monitoring tooling around it

Built with Next.js, MongoDB, Docker, AWS.

Screenshot: The national recruitment dashboard, showing applicant totals and a table of applicants per district (https://kanyeceejaya.github.io/images/census-recruitment.jpg)

#### [UBOS dissemination portal](https://statistics.ubos.org) (2024 to now, data platform)

The public home of the 2024 Census results, down to parish level.

Dashboards, maps and tabulations for the census, the education and aquaculture censuses, and the national standard indicators. I led a team of three on the platform and built the ingestion and reporting pipelines underneath it, including the PDF table extraction that makes decades of survey reports queryable.

- 500,000+: public users
- 3: people on the team I led

Built with Python and SQL pipelines, Power BI, QGIS.

Links: [statistics.ubos.org](https://statistics.ubos.org)

Screenshot: The Census 2024 dashboard on the UBOS portal: total population and household counts above cards for the data explorer, map explorer and visualisation builder (https://kanyeceejaya.github.io/images/shot-portal-nphc.jpg)

#### Also at the Bureau (2023 to now, data work)

Classification, collection tools, GIS tooling, cloud and security.

Automated classification for coding census and survey responses, which removed months of manual work. The data collection instruments used for national enumeration. Python and QGIS tooling that sped up map preparation for the GIS team. The Bureau's AWS and GCP estate, including a shared outbound proxy that consolidated external service access and traffic filtering. Phishing exercises with the security team.

Sign in without passwords, in Flutter.

## Stories behind some of these

### The 4th Industrial Revolution Taskforce

April 2019 to January 2021

In April 2019 President Museveni set up a 21-member expert taskforce, chaired by former ICT minister John Nasasira, to study the technologies of the fourth industrial revolution and advise government on how Uganda should adopt them.

I joined from the Ministry of ICT's Government Citizen Interaction Centre, a few months after finishing university, and met the President with the rest of the team when he launched it.

Over the next eighteen months we studied how other countries were preparing and wrote the report that became Uganda's national 4IR strategy: skills, infrastructure, research, cyber security and data protection, aimed at making Uganda a 4IR hub by 2040. The draft went public in October 2020, and the final report was handed to the Prime Minister in December 2022.

Links: [Read the appointment on the Ministry of ICT site](https://dmu.ict.go.ug/he-museveni-appoints-4th-industrial-revolution-taskforce)

Photo caption: President Museveni talks to Akbr Kanyesigye at the launch, as ICT Minister Frank Tumwebaze looks on. April 2019. Photo: Ministry of ICT and National Guidance.

### Kyankwanzi, 2026

Political Education, Transformative and Leadership Development Course. National Leadership Institute, Kyankwanzi. Completed 30 July 2026.

A residential course for staff of the Bureau, UBOS Intake 04 of 2026: political economy, Uganda's history and its place in the world, leadership, Kiswahili, and military training.

My syndicate's closing paper examined the impact of digital media and artificial intelligence on governance, national security, public opinion and socio-economic development in Uganda. It weighed online services and census tablets against deepfakes, cybercrime and the 2024 breach at the Bank of Uganda.

Along the way I built the intake a small offline revision site, with flashcards, mock exams, a Kiswahili songbook and a shared leaderboard.

Links: [See the paper](https://kanyeceejaya.github.io/#pp-nali), [See it under education](https://kanyeceejaya.github.io/#ed-nali)

## Notes

### Five rules for AI over official statistics

4 August 2026. https://kanyeceejaya.github.io/notes/2026-08-five-rules-for-ai-over-official-statistics.html

Generative systems are arriving in statistical dissemination across the continent this year, often procured quickly and judged more on how fluent they sound than on whether the numbers are right. A model that produces a confident, wrong district population hands the reputational bill to the office that published it. Official statistics carry value only because the public accepts the figure.

So before Sanyu goes out as a public service of the Bureau, we wrote down the conditions we had to meet to feel safe releasing it. Five clauses, each one drawn from something the build itself forced on us. They're short enough to check.

### 1. Figures originate in the statistical system

The model selects what to retrieve; the database supplies the value. A number reaches the user only when a structured query returned it. This is the whole architecture in one sentence. The language model never generates a figure, it emits a typed function call, and the verified result is placed into the answer verbatim.

### 2. Every figure carries its source

Source table, survey or census, reference period and geography travel with the value, in a form the user can follow back to the publication. Charts render from the same verified values as the surrounding text, so a picture can't disagree with its caption.

### 3. The system declines outside its data

Where a question falls beyond published statistics, the correct response says so plainly. Silence about a limit counts as a defect. This one was harder to build than it sounds, because a fluent model would much rather answer.

### 4. Evaluation is published before launch

A named benchmark with ground truth, plus a regression suite that asserts exact published figures, runs automatically on every build. Ours has 45 deterministic tests, including a set of golden facts that must match the printed census tables to the digit. The results are public.

### 5. A statistician signs

Generated narrative passes a named human reviewer before publication. The machine drafts; the office remains the author.

> The code demonstrates that the conditions are achievable, because the system standing beside it meets them.

None of these rules is about a particular vendor or model. They're conditions any statistics office could adopt this year, and we'd like other offices to argue with them, adapt them, and tell us what we missed. The technical details of how Sanyu meets them are on the [work page](https://kanyeceejaya.github.io/#p-sanyu).

### A week in Rome with SDMX

6 October 2025. https://kanyeceejaya.github.io/notes/2025-10-a-week-in-rome-with-sdmx.html

Ivan Atwiine and I spent last week at the 10th SDMX Global Conference in Rome, hosted by the Bank of Italy. Three days of plenaries, then two days of training. The theme was "Smarter data for better insights", and the invitation had asked for exactly the kind of work we do: AI and machine learning applied to statistical pipelines, and dissemination tools that people actually use.

We went to talk about the pipeline. The paper, "From fragmentation to intelligence", describes how UBOS pulls administrative, survey and census data straight from source systems into one platform, validates it on the way in, and publishes it through the national dashboard. The rule-based checks catch the obvious; the machine learning helps with anomalies, cleaning and classifying community-level submissions. It's the plumbing behind everything else the Bureau now does with data.

### What I took home

**SDMX is a join key, not a file format.** I had been treating it as a way to publish. The better way to see it: once two datasets share the same concepts, code lists and dimensions, a question that crosses them becomes cheap to answer. That is precisely what a chatbot over official statistics needs. Most of the effort in grounding a language model is agreeing on what an indicator means, and SDMX is that agreement, written down.

**Validation can be data too.** The sessions on SDMX 3.0 and VTL, the validation and transformation language, described rules as something you exchange rather than something buried in a script. We write ours in Python. Some of them should probably live next to the data instead.

**Everyone's problem is fragmentation.** Central banks, statistical offices, international agencies: the stories differed in scale, not in kind. The exciting demos all rested on the boring, careful part, which is people agreeing on structure. That was reassuring. It is the part we can control.

The two training days made the tooling concrete: data structure definitions, dataflows, registries. It's one thing to read the standard, another to build a dataflow with someone who has done it a hundred times and watch where they slow down.

### What changed back home

We came back and started a prototype: take survey tables from the demographic and health survey and the household survey, and turn them into SDMX-ready structures. Reusable structure definitions by table shape rather than one per table, and a crosswalk of indicators so we can say quickly whether a figure exists in one survey, the other, or both. It's the first step toward cross-dataset retrieval, chatbot queries that span surveys, and briefs that write themselves from verified numbers.

Rome itself: warm, loud, and exactly as good at coffee as advertised.
